z4.note: Plain grey lid over a uniform random speckle of sage leaves (the glass body is not rendered); no label, seam or readable mark anywhere, and the 90-degree tiles are indistinguishable from the original in all six cameras - the survey's blob is only noise-pattern mismatch.

z2.note: End-to-end flip about the vertical: both ends show the same two-lobed quill outline and blunt cut, the bark is a uniform fleck texture with no knot or mark, and the flipped stick looks identical in every camera.

y4.note: Rotation about the long axis: the quill's cross-section is a flattened two-lobed scroll (12 x 8 mm) with a slit groove, so the end-on tiles change from a two-lobed to a rounded outline and the stick's apparent width changes by roughly a quarter - the groove/seam position is readable.

y5.note: Same as y4: the two-lobed scroll cross-section with its slit is not a body of revolution; the 72-degree tiles show a different end outline and a narrower stick from above, so the seam position gives the rotation away.

y6.note: Same as y4: the slit groove of the two-lobed quill moves around the stick under a 60-degree turn, visible as a changed end outline and apparent width in the tiles.

z2.note: The end-to-end flip swaps the sharpened tip (exposed wood cone and dark lead) with the plain yellow blunt end; a person sees at once which end is the point.
One end is sharpened (wood cone and lead), the other is a plain purple blunt end; the z flip puts the tip at the opposite end.

x4.note: Unprinted hexagonal pencil turned about its own axis: only the facet corners move, the blue body, blunt end and sharpened tip look the same in every camera and there is no print or logo.

x5.note: Same as x4: a 72-degree turn about the long axis of an unprinted hexagonal pencil changes nothing a person could read; body and tip look identical.
